entry.title: OpenAI launches Dots, always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra that autonomously handle tasks and integrate with over 4,000 apps across Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise plans [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI introduced Dots, AI agents designed to work continuously on users' behalf by learning preferences and managing tasks autonomously using their own cloud computer and browser. These agents connect with thousands of apps and are accessible via platforms like ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams, aiming to increase productivity by handling work proactively. Dots can independently manage projects, update analyses, automate content production, and adapt to changing requirements across various professional roles. OpenAI is initially rolling out Dots to select subscription plans and markets, with plans to expand availability and develop specialized versions for deeper organizational integration and access management.

entry.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Sol, matching GPT-6 Astra's intelligence on coding and professional tasks at one-fifth the token cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol, an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol that delivers near-GPT-6 Astra intelligence for agentic coding, computer use, and professional work at significantly reduced token prices. The model offers cached input costs at $0.10 per million tokens, which is 95% less than standard input pricing and 50% less than GPT-6 Sol's cached input pricing, enabling developers to build and run capable agents more affordably. GPT-6.1 Sol shows substantial improvements over GPT-6 Sol across complex tasks such as software engineering, professional document understanding, multi-step business workflows, computer application interactions, and scientific research workflows. It approaches GPT-6 Astra's performance in many evaluations while costing roughly one-fifth to one-seventh as much per task. The model also improves factual accuracy, reducing errors by about 32% at low reasoning effort compared to GPT-6 Sol. GPT-6 Astra remains the top performer for the most difficult scientific research tasks.

entry.title: Researchers publish a privacy analysis of web and mobile conversational AI agents, examining data tracking and user information exposure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A new study analyzes the privacy implications of conversational AI agents used on web and mobile platforms, focusing on how these systems collect and handle user data. The research highlights potential risks related to data tracking and information leakage in popular AI assistants. This analysis provides insights into the privacy challenges posed by conversational AI technologies and suggests areas for improving user data protection.

entry.title: Trump signs executive order requiring US government to replace 'artificial intelligence' with 'Super Intelligence' in official documents and communications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: President Donald Trump has issued an executive order directing the US executive branch to stop using the term "artificial intelligence" and instead refer to it as "Super Intelligence" in all official policy websites, documents, and press releases. Trump described "Super Intelligence" as a more accurate and positive term, emphasizing its power and potential for good use while distancing it from the negative connotations of the word "artificial." The order follows a White House luncheon with tech CEOs and government officials, where Trump highlighted the importance of self-regulation and cooperation with local communities for data center development. The administration's move represents a significant shift in terminology, as "Super Intelligence" typically refers to highly advanced AI systems, but the order mandates its use as a replacement for the broader statutory definition of AI. While past regulations and documents will not be changed, US officials are expected to avoid acknowledging the terms "artificial intelligence" or "AI" in relevant contexts going forward. Trump also noted support from Chinese President Xi Jinping for the new terminology, aiming to reduce fears about AI's rapid advancement and safety risks.

entry.title: McDonald's uses AI-driven pricing engine to set dynamic menu prices across US and global locations, raising concerns among franchisees and regulators [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: McDonald's has implemented an AI-powered pricing system that analyzes millions of daily transactions to recommend optimal prices for menu items at nearly 14,000 restaurants. This system creates price variations even between nearby locations and incorporates competitor pricing data, aiming to boost profitability but causing tension with franchisees who report pressure to adopt the AI recommendations. The pricing engine is part of McDonald's broader strategy to balance affordability and profitability, though it faces potential regulatory scrutiny over algorithmic pricing practices and risks alienating customers due to price disparities. Other fast-food chains like Wendy's and Yum Brands have explored or commented on similar AI pricing tools, highlighting industry-wide interest and challenges in dynamic pricing.

entry.title: Dallas councilmember and residents challenge AI-generated blight scores on 21,000 homes amid concerns over fairness and impact on low-income neighborhoods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Dallas has deployed AI-powered cameras on trash trucks to photograph and assign "blight scores" to over 21,000 properties since April, aiming to identify potential code violations. The system has sparked concerns from a city councilmember and residents who worry it may disproportionately affect lower-income neighborhoods and lead to increased fines. Councilmember Chad West proposed halting funding for the $2.5 million, three-year camera program, citing fears it could become a financial burden on struggling homeowners, especially in Southern Dallas. City officials and the camera operator maintain the technology is intended to improve code enforcement efficiency and protect privacy, with human review of images and internal use of blight scores to prioritize inspections. The city has issued about 1,800 courtesy notices so far, encouraging voluntary repairs before enforcement actions.

entry.title: AMD to acquire AI startup World Labs for $8.2 billion, gaining world models technology and research talent to compete with Nvidia [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: AMD announced plans to acquire AI startup World Labs, founded by Fei-Fei Li and others in 2024, in a deal valued at $8.2 billion expected to close by the end of the year pending regulatory approval. The acquisition brings World Labs' expertise in world models-AI systems that simulate physical environments-and its research team under AMD's umbrella, including Li who will become AMD's Executive Vice President and Chief Scientist. World Labs has developed tools like Marble, which generates 3D spaces for content creation, and focuses on applications such as synthetic data generation for robotics training, an area where Nvidia currently leads. AMD aims to leverage World Labs' technology to enhance its AI chip offerings and better compete in the AI hardware market dominated by Nvidia, particularly as AI expands into robotics, simulation, and physical AI workloads.

entry.title: New Zealand teachers' union warns AI marking risks, urges human oversight to maintain assessment quality and fairness
entry.summary: A New Zealand teachers' union has raised concerns about the increasing use of AI for grading student work, emphasizing that AI should assist rather than replace teachers in marking. The union highlighted that while AI marking has achieved over 80% agreement with human markers in some tests, it is less reliable for complex assessments and could compromise fairness and professional judgment. The union's report noted that AI marking has reduced the number of human check markers significantly and is expected to expand under the new qualification system planned for 2028-2030. However, it stressed that teacher involvement in marking is crucial for maintaining standards, understanding student work, and ensuring assessment integrity. The union advocates for a hybrid model where AI supports teachers but human professionals retain accountability for grading decisions.

entry.title: America.gov chatbot recites Minecraft End Poem as an intentional easter egg, not a glitch [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The U.S. government launched the America.gov AI chatbot in partnership with Google and SpaceXAI, which responds unusually when asked about Minecraft by reciting a poetic monologue based on the game's End Poem. This behavior is a deliberate easter egg rather than a malfunction, reflecting a creative integration within the chatbot's design. The poem, originally written by Julian Gough for Minecraft, is adapted by the chatbot into a message blending government themes and existential reflections. The chatbot has proven resistant to jailbreak attempts and includes accurate political facts, indicating careful engineering behind its responses. This unexpected feature highlights a unique intersection of government technology and cultural references.

entry.title: Oura delays IPO amid broader market stall affecting companies like Amaero and Holtec Nuclear
entry.summary: Oura, a fitness ring maker, has postponed its initial public offering due to uncertainty in the IPO market, reflecting a wider slowdown that has also impacted metals producer Amaero and Holtec Nuclear Corp. The stalled IPO environment is influenced by factors such as rising energy costs, trade tensions, military conflicts, increasing interest rates, and uncertainties in data center development. Meanwhile, SB Energy, a SoftBank-controlled power developer for data centers, has filed IPO paperwork but has not yet started marketing the offering.

entry.title: Trump and leading AI executives sign voluntary safety accord with four layers of controls and plan to form oversight committee [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: President Trump and executives from major AI companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, and SpaceX signed a voluntary agreement establishing safety standards for AI development, described by Trump as "morally binding." The accord commits companies to implement four layers of controls and audits, conduct regular meetings to set standards, and consider future legal codification of these measures. Trump also announced plans to appoint an "AI czar" and directed the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence. The agreement follows growing concerns about AI safety risks, with some industry leaders calling for slower development while others emphasize innovation alongside safety. Trump favors voluntary self-regulation over stricter government rules, citing economic growth and competition with China. However, some lawmakers, including Senator Mark Warner, have criticized the voluntary approach and called for mandatory AI testing and reporting regulations.

entry.title: UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs launch Inspect, an open-source framework for evaluating large language models with over 200 pre-built benchmarks and multi-agent support [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Inspect is an open-source evaluation framework developed by the UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs to assess large language models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, behavior, and multi-modal tasks. It offers composable components like datasets, agents, tools, and scorers, along with a web-based interface and VS Code extension for monitoring and authoring evaluations. The framework supports over 20 model providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and HuggingFace, and enables flexible tool calling and sandboxed execution of untrusted code. Users can run existing benchmarks or create custom evaluations involving single-turn generation or multi-agent interactions, with examples such as question-answering and capture-the-flag challenges provided.

entry.title: SpaceXAI's AI-powered Grokipedia resumes article updates after months-long pause, with recent fact-checks and user suggestions accepted [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Grokipedia, the AI-driven encyclopedia developed by SpaceXAI and associated with Elon Musk, has resumed updating its articles after a pause of several months. Recent activity includes fact-checking of pages like Barack Obama and Elon Musk, as well as acceptance of user-submitted updates such as a video game release date. While some pages remain outdated, the platform's live update site shows ongoing edits and reviews. The site had not reviewed edits since April, according to a previous report, but now displays recent changes, including notes to recheck references. SpaceXAI has not commented on the renewed activity, and Elon Musk has not posted about Grokipedia since early 2026. Benji Taylor, head of design at X and SpaceXAI, indicated that a new version of Grokipedia is forthcoming, suggesting continued development despite the earlier inactivity.

entry.title: Modal and Carnegie Mellon researchers launch Quail to jointly optimize AI-SQL query planning and inference engine, achieving over 1 billion tokens per minute per H100 GPU [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Modal and Carnegie Mellon University's Full Stack Data Lab developed Quail, an inference engine that accelerates AI-SQL queries by jointly optimizing the query planner and inference process. Quail achieves more than 10 times the speed of previous baselines on the same hardware, processing over a billion tokens per minute per H100 GPU, reducing costs to under 6 cents per billion tokens on Modal's platform. Quail improves efficiency by leveraging structured query information to better manage key-value caching and reduce host overhead, particularly for workloads involving many small requests and smaller models. The project represents a collaboration between inference and database researchers aiming to enhance performance engineering at the intersection of AI inference and database systems, with code and benchmarks publicly available for further exploration.

entry.title: Cache Invalidation Simulator [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
How Investors Are Financing On-Site Power to Break AI Bottlenecks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Companies building and operating data centers are hungry for ways to secure the power needed to move ahead with massive AI build-outs. That's prompted big financing pledges and creative dealmaking for on-site power that can cut data centers' reliance on electric grids. Investors are getting in on the crunch through several angles, including large investments in specific projects, such as new on-site power plants. Some investors are also taking equity stakes in companies that provide on-site power, or providing outside capital to finance equipment like fuel cells for end customers such as AI cloud providers. A Blackstone-led group, including KKR and Apollo, this summer agreed to invest $5.3 billion for a 49% stake in five gas-fired power projects pipeline giant Williams is developing to supply on-site power for data centers. Of the $5.3 billion, $4.4 billion will cover the investors' share of expected project costs, Williams said. Though on-site power can be pricier than connecting to the grid, availability and speed is an obvious advantage. Williams, which recently expanded into developing and running on-site generation for data centers, said last month it brought its first 200 megawatts online less than 18 months after commercialization. By comparison, Fitch Ratings estimates that building new infrastructure such as grid-connected power plants and high-voltage transmission lines can take five to 10 years. Many power-generation deals have been financed primarily on a project-by-project basis. But some investors have also started buying stakes in companies that provide on-site power generation, whether that be gas plants, fuel cells or solar projects, giving investors exposure to broader growth rather than a specific project. For instance, Blackstone and Halliburton in May announced a $1 billion equity investment in VoltaGrid, which builds and operates on-site gas-powered systems for data centers. "With all the private equity and other money that has come into the market, there's different structures. And when there's private equity, they want to have an ownership interest in the developer entity," said Carl Bivens, a real estate partner at Troutman Pepper Locke. Meanwhile, the up-front costs of bringing power on-site to data centers quickly has created a need for outside capital to provide financing for customers such as smaller AI cloud providers. That's similar to other areas in AI infrastructure, where some cloud providers have been relying on special purpose vehicles that use outside capital to finance expensive assets like graphics processing units. On the power side, Bloom Energy announced last fall that Brookfield Asset Management had agreed to provide up to $5 billion to finance future power projects for AI data centers, with Bloom providing the fuel cells. In June, Bloom announced that Brookfield had expanded the amount of potential financing to $25 billion. Bloom has relied for more than a decade on infrastructure funds and investment firms to form SPVs that finance deployments of its products, but investor interest accelerated more recently, a person familiar with the financings said. Investors are also financing on-site power projects for Bloom customers, separately from the broader Brookfield framework. In July, project developer Industrial Development Funding and investment firm Oaktree Capital Management announced a $1.7 billion project investment to install Bloom fuel cells at Nebius data centers. Oaktree is contributing minority equity financing, with MUFG leading senior debt financing, while Nebius will pay Bloom for power. But the rush of financing for on-site power creates a potential timing mismatch across different parts of what's needed to get an AI data center up and running. Some power assets can operate for decades, while big AI compute contracts are often much shorter and the GPUs inside data centers can become outdated in just a few years. For developers and the investors financing power infrastructure, longer contracts that lock in predictable cash flow are preferable. Investors are pushing for longer customer commitments to underpin these deals, increasingly favoring 10- to 15-year commitments from large cloud providers with five-year renewal options, Bivens said. "It provides a longer runway of guaranteed rent for the investors. It allows [institutional investors] to amortize their costs of the behind-the-meter solution or the data center build," he said. Customers of the on-site power may want more flexibility, particularly if they're awaiting grid power. That points to the bigger question of how much data centers will need to rely on on-site power in the long term. For example, more grid power could become available or GPUs could become more energy efficient, and data centers' on-site power needs might evolve by the time big contracts expire. Industrial Development Funding, an infrastructure investment firm and the developer behind the Bloom-Nebius project, says on-site power projects can still be valuable even if the data centers' power needs themselves change. The owners of the project could sell power into broader markets down the line, said IDF CEO Nik Nunes. For instance, if a data center tenant moves on when its initial contract term ends, the power asset could be mostly paid off but could still generate revenue. "If I have a power block that is significantly amortized in six to eight years, I have a lot of optionality to sell that power into the grid or into other markets," Nunes said. Converting to Convertibles Convertible bonds have been one particularly popular way for tech companies to raise cash in a banner year for financing across the sector, fueled by the AI build-out. Technology companies have accounted for about 60% of overall U.S. convertible bond issuance so far in 2026, raising roughly $78 billion through Sept. 11, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. That's up from around 44% of that market last year. By comparison, tech companies accounted for 50% of equity follow-on offerings, 27% of investment-grade debt and 20% of high-yield issuance so far this year. The convertible surge comes as financing costs for AI-specific debt have been rising. Investors are swamped with new supply and grappling with uncertainties about how AI investments will pay off. Convertible debt often carries lower coupons than straight corporate bonds since investors get an upside if the stock rises. That can eventually dilute the holdings of existing shareholders, but potentially less so than equity offerings. "Obviously, there's the benefits of being not as dilutive as a follow-on. So it has been one of the places of priority," Chris Fenske, head of capital markets research at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said on a webinar last week. And S&P Global's total doesn't count recent convertible issuance like CoreWeave's $4.2 billion sale last week. But as more companies tap convertibles, that form of financing too could get more expensive-we'll see whether those firms shift to equity raises next. Microsoft Tears Down Its AI Data Wall [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Microsoft's biggest products have generally thrived by letting other companies build on top of them. So Microsoft's decision to join Apache Ossie, a 1-year-old software industry group aiming to make it easier for AI tools to access data from applications and databases, might not seem like a big deal. But actually it is. Just four months ago, Microsoft moved to block partners from connecting their data management tools to Microsoft's Power BI, which companies use to analyze data in charts and graphs. In doing so, Microsoft appeared to be protecting its own data management product, Fabric, at the expense of rival firms such as Databricks and Snowflake. In other words, Microsoft was opening a new front in the AI data wars, part of traditional enterprise app firms' efforts to stop customers from using AI from other companies to access data they store in traditional apps. After our report in May, Microsoft took heat for its decision. We don't know what's happened behind the scenes since then, but the company must have had a change of heart. And its decision to join Ossie is in line with CEO Satya Nadella's strategy of building products that worked those of rivals, such as developing a mobile version of Office for Apple iOS and Google's Android operating systems over a decade ago. Salesforce made a similar transition in the past couple of years and now is making it easy for customers to use AI tools such as Claude to access their Salesforce data-for a price.

entry.title: Use Google Gemini to Research Vendor Products, Services, and Features [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Making a vendor recommendation for a major IT initiative can be paralyzing. Every company promises a "seamless" user experience and "robust" APIs, but buyers typically lack visibility into real-world implementation and operations until after they've already made a decision. As a result, many tech leaders default to recommendations from people in their networks, or even avoid making a change at all, preferring to stick with the "devil they know" over risking the unknown. Google Gemini can help you quickly research vendor products, services, and features, going beyond the marketing materials to surface real-world insights about implementation, integration, and total cost of ownership. Step 1: Vent Your Frustrations Open up a new chat in Gemini and list off everything that is driving you mad about your current product or platform so Gemini has comprehensive context about the problem you are looking to solve. If you're looking for a new cloud vendor, the problem might be unpredictable costs, or it might be unacceptable levels of latency. Those are two very different problems, and each might be best solved by two different vendors. Don't sugar-coat here. Mention user adoption issues, unhelpful account managers, broken integrations, and anything else that has you considering a change. If Gemini knows what's currently going wrong, it will be better equipped to make best-fit recommendations. Step 2: Generate Recommendations Give Gemini some basic background information about your company and what technology you're looking to replace. Include your frustrations from Step 1. Here's a sample prompt: I am the CIO at [company]. We are currently evaluating vendor options to [replatform our intranet]. Right now, we use [vendor], but we are looking to switch because [we are unhappy with limited functionality and account support]. Suggest additional vendor options to consider and include descriptions of their product and services and key features. Gemini will evaluate the scope of the change you are looking to make, consider your specific context, and offer several options. If you explain that you lead the IT department at a global supply chain company with 14,000 employees, for example, Gemini will account for organization-specific considerations like mobile access and integration with shift-scheduling systems. Review Gemini's initial shortlist to identify top contenders, eliminate any obvious mismatches, and move forward with your finalists. Step 3: Dig Deeper Gemini's initial responses will focus on the hero features and selling points of several options, drawing from various sources, including vendors' own marketing materials. This means you may need to continue the conversation to fully address potential friction points like integration, pricing issues, and scalability challenges. Follow up with Gemini, this time asking it to take a more skeptical look at your top choices. Here, you can ask pointed questions about specific details and more fully explore likely total costs. You can even prompt Gemini to scour the web for user reviews, helping you to discover stories from previous customers who had subpar experiences. Try prompts like these: What are some of the known integration challenges when connecting [Vendor] to [System A] and [System B]? Summarize the three most common complaints that enterprise IT teams express about [Vendor's] technical performance or customer service. What is the realistic enterprise deployment timeline for [Vendor], as opposed to their estimated sales timeline? Are there any configuration issues I should watch out for? By asking these types of questions, you can push Gemini to go beyond generic feature lists and give you more granular information that gets you closer to a decision. Step 4: Compare and Contrast Chat with Gemini for a bit. Go back-and-forth until you feel like you have a comprehensive understanding of the benefits and potential tradeoffs for each vendor, including how each will fit with your existing environment. Then, ask Gemini to summarize its findings in a structured table. Try this prompt: Create a matrix comparing [Vendor A] and [Vendor B] across deployment timeline, integration complexity, and potential friction points. Gemini will generate a clean table that helps you cut through the weeds of your sprawling research session, take a big-picture view of your options, and more clearly how vendors compare with one another on your most important criteria. You and your team will still need to make the final recommendation to your leadership team. But now, you will have the real-world information you need to help you make (and defend) your choice.

entry.title: General Catalyst Backs Coding Data Startup Proximal As It Reaches Revenue Milestone [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: It's no secret that leading AI developers are on the hunt for data to improve their models, especially in lucrative areas like software engineering. The insatiable appetite for data has lifted a whole host of so-called data labeling or data curation startups, including older ones like Scale and Surge and newer ones such as Fleet and Micro1. The latest beneficiary is San Francisco-based Proximal, which is coming out of stealth with $15 million in seed funding led by General Catalyst at a $300 million valuation, the company told The Information exclusively. Proximal raised its seed round at the end of last year, when it was generating a negligible amount of revenue, co-founder and CEO Calvin Chen said. Chen had cofounded the 40-person startup last fall with his roommate Justus Mattern, who previously worked at compute startup Prime Intellect, which itself is only two years old. Now, just 10 months later, the company has surpassed $200 million in annualized revenue, he said. (Proximal calculates annualized revenue by taking the revenue generated in the quarter so far and multiplying it by four, Chen said.)
